new_statements.quote: Runyankore is both a tonal language and a syllable-timed language, meaning that every syllable tends to be produced with roughly equal duration and tone (Poletto, 1998). In contrast, English is stress-timed, with rhythm determined by the timing of stressed syllables and a greater use of intonation for pragmatic and emotional meaning. [...] Participants in this study fail to acquire the prosodic rules needed for native-like English fluency because Runyankore does not rely on stress-based rhythm or intonation contours in the same way English does.
new_statements.citation: Nuwahereza, Allan. 2025. Mother tongue interference in the speaking of English among L1 Runyankore-speaking students of Makerere University. Unpublished MA dissertation, Makerere University, Kampala (MakIR hdl 10570/15414).
new_statements.locator: Section 5.2.4 'Tonal and syllable-timed prosody', printed pp. 64-65 (PDF pp. 74-75)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Runyankore is described as a tone language (H, L, falling per Ndoleriire 2024 as cited) that is syllable-timed and has no stress-based rhythm; nothing is said about a fixed word-stress position. The only first-hand prosodic facts in the opened primary sources (Poletto 1998 WPL; Hyman 2022 SPiL Plus) are tonal: falling tones are confined to a long phrase-penultimate syllable and final H retracts to the penult phrase-finally.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about utterance rhythm (syllable-timing) in L2-English interference, not word-level citation forms; second-hand, attributed to Poletto 1998 whose dissertation could not be opened. Treat as weak.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Runyankore (Nkore) proper or the joint standard Runyankore-Rukiga; Nkore-Kiga (Taylor 1985) covers Nkore and Kiga (chig1238) together. The Makerere theses treat 'Runyankore' as spoken in Ankole (Mbarara etc.), i.e. nyan1307.

sources.note: Sec. 5.2.4 'Tonal and syllable-timed prosody', pp. 64-65: Runyankore is a tonal, syllable-timed language with roughly equal syllable duration (citing Poletto 1998) and 'does not rely on stress-based rhythm or intonation contours in the same way English does'; no statement on word-stress position. Second-hand; applied-linguistics MA, not a phonological description.
